meta.title: Immediate Life Support (adult) topic map
meta.based_on: Resuscitation Council UK ILS learning outcomes and 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines summary; Sonal's own ILS notes (ILS.docx)
meta.warning: Reference facts are written for study use and must be checked by a qualified clinician against the current RCUK ILS manual before wide use.

mastery_scale.5: Mastered: right on 3 or more separate days, including scenario questions

domains.name: Recognising and treating the deteriorating patient
Causes and prevention of cardiac arrest
ALS algorithm, drugs and reversible causes
Non-technical skills, post-arrest care and decisions

topics.name: The ABCDE approach
objectives: Assess and treat in order A, B, C, D, E
key_facts: Assess Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure in order and treat each problem as you find it before moving on.
Re-assess the patient after every intervention and whenever their condition changes.
Signs of airway obstruction include see-saw (paradoxical) chest movement, noisy breathing such as stridor or gurgling, and accessory muscle use. Complete obstruction is silent.
Breathing assessment covers respiratory rate, work of breathing, SpO2, chest expansion, percussion and auscultation.
Circulation assessment covers pulse rate and rhythm, blood pressure, capillary refill time (normal is 2 seconds or less), skin colour and temperature, and urine output.
Disability covers AVPU or GCS, pupils, blood glucose, and drug causes such as opioids.
Exposure means examining the whole body for bleeding, rashes or wounds while protecting dignity and preventing heat loss.
common_mistakes: Skipping ahead to circulation before fixing the airway
Forgetting to check blood glucose in D
Not re-assessing after treatment

topics.name: Oxygen therapy and targets
key_facts: In critical illness, give high-concentration oxygen initially using a non-rebreather mask with reservoir at 15 L/min.
The usual target SpO2 is 94 to 98 percent.
For patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD, target 88 to 92 percent.
Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient in a peri-arrest or arrest situation.
common_mistakes: Applying the 88 to 92 percent target to every COPD patient without assessing risk
Withholding oxygen from a critically ill hypoxic patient

topics.name: Early warning scores and escalation (NEWS2, SBAR)
key_facts: NEWS2 scores respiratory rate, SpO2, use of supplemental oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, level of consciousness or new confusion, and temperature.
A score of 3 in any single parameter needs urgent review by a clinician.
A total score of 5 or more is a key threshold for urgent response, and 7 or more needs an emergency response, often including critical care outreach.
SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation and gives a structured way to escalate.
The 2025 guidelines emphasise early warning scores, critical care outreach, and routes for patients and families to escalate concerns.
common_mistakes: Ignoring a single red parameter because the total is low
Escalating without a clear recommendation or request

topics.name: Causes and prevention of in-hospital cardiac arrest
key_facts: Most in-hospital cardiac arrests are preceded by a period of physiological deterioration, often hypoxia and hypotension, that is missed or poorly treated.
In UK hospitals the most common first rhythm in adult in-hospital arrest is PEA (about 52 percent), then asystole (about 20 percent), then VF/pVT (about 18 percent), per RCUK 2025 data.
Survival to discharge is much higher for shockable rhythms (about 53 percent for VF/pVT) than for PEA (about 17 percent) or asystole (about 12 percent).
The chain of prevention covers staff education, monitoring, recognition, calling for help, and an effective response.
Patients unlikely to benefit from CPR should have resuscitation decisions discussed and recorded in advance, for example with ReSPECT.
common_mistakes: Assuming most in-hospital arrests are VF
Seeing arrest as sudden and unpredictable

topics.name: Recognising cardiac arrest and the in-hospital response
objectives: Know the first actions in hospital
key_facts: Check for a response, shout for help, open the airway, and look for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. A trained person may check a carotid pulse at the same time.
Agonal (occasional, gasping) breathing is a sign of cardiac arrest and must not be mistaken for normal breathing.
In hospital, call the resuscitation team (for example 2222 in the UK) and send for the defibrillator and resuscitation equipment.
Start CPR immediately if there are no signs of life and attach the defibrillator as soon as possible.
First make sure the environment is safe, then approach the patient.
Check for a response by gently shaking the shoulders and asking loudly 'Are you alright?'. If there's no response, shout for help or pull the emergency buzzer.
Turn the patient onto their back, open the airway with head tilt and chin lift, then LOOK for chest movement, LISTEN for breath sounds and FEEL for air on your cheek, for less than 10 seconds.
Call 2222 for the resuscitation team in hospital, or 999 out of hospital.

If help has arrived, start CPR and send the helper to call the team and bring the equipment. If you are alone, leave the patient to summon help and collect the equipment, then return as soon as possible to start CPR.
common_mistakes: Treating agonal breaths as normal breathing
Delaying CPR to search for a pulse for longer than 10 seconds
Forgetting to check the environment is safe first

topics.name: High-quality chest compressions
objectives: Know rate, depth, ratio and recoil
key_facts: Compress in the centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum) at 100 to 120 per minute and 5 to 6 cm deep.
Allow full chest recoil after each compression and minimise interruptions.
Without an advanced airway, use a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 ventilations.
Change the person doing compressions about every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue.
Each ventilation should take about 1 second and produce visible chest rise.
Hand position: heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
Keep your arms straight with your shoulders vertically above the patient's chest.
common_mistakes: Compressing too fast or too shallow
Leaning on the chest so it can't recoil
Long pauses for tasks
Bending the elbows, which gives shallow compressions

topics.name: Airway manoeuvres, adjuncts and ventilation
key_facts: Simple manoeuvres are head tilt and chin lift, or jaw thrust when cervical spine injury is suspected.
Size an oropharyngeal airway by measuring from the incisors to the angle of the jaw. Don't use one in a patient with an intact gag reflex.
A nasopharyngeal airway is often tolerated by semi-conscious patients, used with caution in suspected basal skull fracture.
A supraglottic airway such as an i-gel can be used during CPR. If it seals well, give continuous compressions with about 10 ventilations per minute.
Waveform capnography confirms airway placement, monitors CPR quality, and a sudden rise in ETCO2 can indicate ROSC.
The 2025 guidelines put greater emphasis on effective ventilation during resuscitation.
common_mistakes: Over-ventilating once an advanced airway is in
Using an OPA in a patient who gags

topics.name: Safe defibrillation (manual and AED)
objectives: Deliver a shock safely with minimal pause
key_facts: Place pads in the anterolateral position: one below the right clavicle, the other at the left mid-axillary line (V6 position). The 2025 guidelines stress correct pad placement.
Keep pauses in compressions before and after a shock as short as possible, ideally under 5 seconds.
Charge the defibrillator during compressions, then pause briefly to confirm the rhythm and deliver the shock.
Remove oxygen at least 1 metre from the chest during the shock and make sure nobody is touching the patient.
Give the first biphasic shock at the energy recommended by the manufacturer (often 150 to 200 J) and consider increasing energy for later shocks if the device allows.
Resume compressions immediately after a shock without checking the rhythm or pulse.
Up to three quick successive (stacked) shocks may be considered for witnessed, monitored VF/pVT when a defibrillator is immediately available, such as in a cardiac catheter lab.
Pad placement from the notes: one pad below the right clavicle, the other directly below the left armpit in the mid-axillary line.
As soon as the defibrillator is attached, do a rhythm check, pausing compressions for no longer than 5 seconds.

With a manual defibrillator, the team leader tells everyone except the person doing compressions to 'stand clear' and remove any oxygen delivery device. A designated team member selects the energy and charges.
Once charged, the person doing compressions is told to 'stand clear'. When everyone is clear, the shock is delivered.
With an AED, follow the machine's audio and visual prompts for prompt, safe shock delivery.
After the shock, continue CPR for a full 2-minute cycle and don't stop unless the patient shows obvious signs of life. The team leader prepares the team for the next rhythm check.
common_mistakes: Checking for a pulse straight after the shock
Leaving oxygen near the chest
Long pauses while charging

topics.name: Cardiac arrest rhythms
key_facts: Shockable rhythms are ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT).
Non-shockable rhythms are pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole.
PEA is organised electrical activity on the monitor without a palpable pulse or signs of life.
Check the rhythm about every 2 minutes. Only check for a pulse if there is an organised rhythm that could produce an output.
Check leads and gain before diagnosing asystole, and look for P waves because ventricular standstill may respond to pacing.
VF: a bizarre irregular waveform with no recognisable QRS complexes, random frequency and amplitude, and uncoordinated electrical activity. It can be coarse or fine.
Before calling VF, exclude artefact from movement or electrical interference.
pVT: a broad-complex rhythm at a rapid rate with constant QRS morphology. Check for a pulse.
PEA: clinical features of cardiac arrest with an ECG that would normally be associated with an output.
Asystole: absent ventricular (QRS) activity. Atrial activity (P waves) may persist, and it is rarely a perfectly straight line.
common_mistakes: Shocking asystole or PEA
Calling fine VF asystole without checking leads and gain
Mistaking movement artefact for VF

topics.name: The adult ALS algorithm and drugs
objectives: Follow the shockable and non-shockable pathways
key_facts: Shockable pathway: shock, then 2 minutes of CPR, then rhythm check, repeating as needed.
In shockable rhythms, give adrenaline 1 mg IV or IO after the third shock, then every 3 to 5 minutes.
In shockable rhythms, give amiodarone 300 mg IV or IO after the third shock, and a further 150 mg after the fifth shock.
In non-shockable rhythms, give adrenaline 1 mg IV or IO as soon as access is gained, then every 3 to 5 minutes. The 2025 guidelines keep early adrenaline for non-shockable rhythms.
Use IV access first. Use intraosseous (IO) access if IV access is difficult or impossible.
If ROSC occurs, begin post-resuscitation care using an ABCDE approach.
Prepare adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg (IV or IO) so they can be given straight after the third shock, once prescribed.
After the first dose, further adrenaline 1 mg is given after alternate shocks, which is about every 3 to 5 minutes.

If a rhythm compatible with a pulse is seen, or the AED advises no shock, check for signs of life. If there are none, continue CPR on the non-shockable side of the algorithm. If there are signs of life, start post-resuscitation care.
common_mistakes: Giving adrenaline before the third shock in VF
Forgetting the second amiodarone dose
Delaying adrenaline in PEA or asystole
Continuing on the shockable side after the rhythm becomes non-shockable

topics.name: Reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts)
objectives: List and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts
key_facts: The 4 Hs are Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo- or hyperkalaemia and other metabolic disorders, and Hypothermia or hyperthermia.
The 4 Ts are Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary), Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), and Toxins.
Consider the reversible causes during every cycle of CPR and use point-of-care ultrasound if a skilled operator is available.
If pulmonary embolism is the suspected cause, consider thrombolysis and continue CPR for 60 to 90 minutes afterwards.
The 2025 guidelines suggest considering extracorporeal CPR in specialist centres for selected refractory arrests, such as hypothermia, thrombosis or toxins.
Hypoxia means low oxygen levels in the body and brain. Hypovolaemia means severe loss of blood or fluid.
Hypo- or hyperkalaemia and other metabolic problems (such as acidosis or abnormal blood glucose) disturb the heart rhythm through abnormal electrolytes.
Thrombosis means a clot in the lungs (pulmonary embolism) or heart (coronary thrombosis). Tamponade is fluid in the pericardial sac stopping the heart filling and beating properly.
Toxins include drug overdoses, poisonings and accidental ingestions. Tension pneumothorax is trapped air in the chest putting pressure on the heart and lungs.
common_mistakes: Only thinking of the reversible causes at the end
Mixing up the Hs and the Ts

topics.name: Peri-arrest emergencies
objectives: Recognise and start treatment of common peri-arrest conditions
key_facts: Adverse features in peri-arrest arrhythmias are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure.
For bradycardia with adverse features, give atropine 500 micrograms IV, repeated up to a maximum of 3 mg, and get expert help for pacing if needed.
For anaphylaxis in adults, give adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) intramuscularly, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
For hypoglycaemia in a patient who can't swallow safely, give IV glucose such as 10 percent glucose, or glucagon 1 mg IM if there is no IV access.
common_mistakes: Giving anaphylaxis adrenaline IV in the ward setting
Under-dosing atropine (less than 500 micrograms)

topics.name: Immediate post-resuscitation care
objectives: Know the first priorities after ROSC
key_facts: After ROSC use an ABCDE approach, protect the airway, and give controlled oxygen with a target SpO2 of 94 to 98 percent.
Aim for normal carbon dioxide levels (normocapnia).
The 2025 target is a systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg or a MAP of 60 to 65 mmHg.
Get a 12-lead ECG. Patients with ST elevation or strong suspicion of coronary occlusion should be considered for urgent coronary angiography.
Prevent fever (keep temperature at or below 37.5 degrees C) in comatose patients.
Hand over to the receiving team using a structured method.
After ROSC: reassess with ABCDE, aim for SpO2 94 to 98 percent and a normal PaCO2, record a 12-lead ECG, treat any precipitating cause, and consider temperature management.
common_mistakes: Giving 100 percent oxygen indefinitely after ROSC
Forgetting the 12-lead ECG

topics.name: Team leadership and teamwork
objectives: Lead or work in a resus team
key_facts: A team leader allocates roles, keeps an overview, plans ahead, and avoids doing hands-on tasks if possible.
Use closed-loop communication: give a clear instruction to a named person, who confirms when it is done.
Situational awareness and sharing the mental model with the team help prevent errors.
Use a pre-shock safety check and say each step out loud.
The 2025 guidelines encourage data-driven debriefing after resuscitation attempts to improve team performance.
Families may be offered the chance to be present during resuscitation, with a staff member supporting them.
Good teamwork means knowing the team's names, supporting each other in your roles, and communicating clearly, including asking for help and raising concerns.
A team leader leads by example and integrity, which needs experience, not just seniority.

Attributes of a good team leader: credibility (knowledge, skills, experience, a good role model), high situational awareness, oversight of timely, safe and effective interventions, strong communication including closed-loop communication, and the ability to delegate appropriately.
common_mistakes: The leader doing compressions and losing the overview
Giving instructions to nobody in particular
Assuming the most senior person automatically makes the best leader

topics.name: Situational awareness, decision making and workload management
objectives: Describe the non-technical skills used at a cardiac arrest
key_facts: The four non-technical skills are situational awareness, decision making, teamwork including leadership, and workload management.
Situational awareness is knowing what is happening around you and understanding how your actions will change things. It matters when many people and events are involved at once.
Establish succinct information early: History (events before the arrest), Diagnosis (confirm cardiac arrest), Team (who is present and their skills), Action (priorities and immediate actions).

Decision making is choosing the right intervention at the right time after gathering information. It is mostly done by the team leader with the team's support. Examples are confirming arrest, calling for help, starting CPR, and attaching the defibrillator and shocking.

Workload management (planning, coordinating and controlling the team's actions) is the team leader's responsibility. It includes prioritising tasks and preparing for both expected and unexpected events.

At an arrest, workload management includes making sure everyone is safe before a shock, managing conflict, watching for fatigue and stress and rotating compressors, offering family support and the chance to be present, debriefing, and completing audit and incident reports.
common_mistakes: Forgetting debriefing and incident reporting as part of the leader's role
Confusing situational awareness with decision making

topics.name: Resuscitation decisions and ethics
key_facts: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR. All other appropriate treatment continues.
ReSPECT records a person's preferences and clinical recommendations for emergency care, including CPR.
Decisions to stop resuscitation are made by the team leader after discussion with the team, considering the patient's wishes, the cause, and the likelihood of success.
Recognise CPR-induced consciousness. The 2025 guidelines suggest managing it with sedation and analgesia given by experienced staff.
common_mistakes: Thinking DNACPR means no treatment at all
